subtype: Approach: imagining the stage and how he will walk in [Thinking]
passage:
Backstage, Rashmi Ma'am found Rishabh standing with his eyes shut in the wings.
Rashmi: Are you all right?
Rishabh: I'm walking, ma'am. Out of the curtain, ten steps to the red spot, stop, feet together.
Rashmi: And then?
Rishabh: I look at the back row, take one breath and say the first line. In my head, it's already happened.
Rashmi: Why do it in your head?
Rishabh: Because when it's the real one, I won't be surprised by anything. I've been there before.
Irawati whispered from the curtain, "Two minutes!" Rishabh opened his eyes and nodded.

qa.q: How many steps does Rishabh count to the red spot?
qa.a: Rishabh counts ten steps to the red spot.

qa.q: What does Rishabh feel about the real moment because of his picture in his head?
qa.a: Rishabh feels calmer and readier, since picturing each step means the real moment holds fewer surprises.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Rishabh use, and why?
qa.a: Rishabh could walk the real stage once before the show or rehearse with friends watching. Being on the real spot gives even more certainty than imagining.

qa.q: How might Irawati see Rishabh's imagining?
qa.a: Irawati whispered that two minutes remained, so Irawati may see Rishabh as calm and ready, and be reassured by that.

grounding: A child closes his eyes and pictures walking on to the stage, standing at the spot and beginning, so the real moment feels less surprising.

subtype: Approach: imagining the stage and how he will walk in [Thinking]
passage: The night before the Republic Day speech, I couldn't sleep, so I tried what my sister Jasleen does before exams. I closed my eyes and pictured it all. The side curtain, the smell of dust on the stage. My name being called: "Gautam, Class 5." Walking out, ten steps, to the chalk cross in the middle. Turning. Looking at the back wall, where the clock is. Breathing in. Saying the first line: "Good morning, respected Principal." I did it three times, each time slower. When I opened my eyes, my heart was still thumping, but the stage felt like somewhere I had already been. Next morning, when they called my name, my feet already knew the ten steps.

qa.q: How many steps did Gautam picture from the curtain to the chalk cross?
qa.a: Gautam pictured ten steps to the chalk cross.

qa.q: How did Gautam feel after imagining the walk three times?
qa.a: Gautam still felt nervous, with a thumping heart, but calmer and more familiar with the stage.

qa.q: What else could Gautam do before the day to make the walk feel real?
qa.a: Gautam could walk the ten steps on the actual stage during rehearsal, so the picture in the head matches the real place.

qa.q: How might Jasleen see Gautam using the exam trick?
qa.a: Jasleen would probably be pleased and a bit proud that the trick helped with a speech too.

grounding: It shows a child picturing each step of walking onto the stage and starting, so the real moment feels less surprising.

subtype: Approach: imagining the stage and how he will walk in [Thinking]
passage:
Teacher's note, Annual Day preparations, Class 4
Sumit is one of our narrators and has been very nervous at rehearsals. Yesterday I found him sitting behind the stage with his eyes closed and his lips moving. I thought he was praying. When I asked, he said, "I'm walking in, ma'am, in my head. Curtain, three steps, microphone, look at the clock at the back." He did it twice more and then did it for real on the stage. His voice was clearer than in any rehearsal so far. Today I let the whole narrators' group sit for two quiet minutes before the run-through to picture their entrances. Sumit showed the others how.
- Ayesha, Class 4 teacher

qa.q: What did Sumit picture looking at from the microphone?
qa.a: He pictured looking at the clock at the back.

qa.q: How was Sumit feeling before he started picturing his entrance?
qa.a: He was very nervous, which is why he was quietly practising behind the stage.

qa.q: What other approach could help a narrator who finds picturing hard?
qa.a: A real walk-through on the empty stage would help, because doing the steps gives the same practice without needing to imagine.

qa.q: How does Sumit's trick look to the teacher?
qa.a: The teacher first thinks he is praying, then sees it works and makes it part of rehearsal for the whole group.

grounding: It shows a child imagining each step onto the stage and the start of his lines, so the real moment surprises him less.
